title: Navigating New Horizons: Charting the Future of Writing Instruction
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky concludes his year-end review by setting out how writing instruction should adapt to generative AI in schools. He argues that students need persuasive, evidence-based rationales rather than prohibitions or utopian hype, and proposes that unassisted writing is more knowledge-constituting, an appeal to immediate benefit rather than future jobs. He supports this with an informal experiment in which the class that avoided research tools generated more original evidence, and with the observation that his students distrust LLMs for college essays. He sees real promise for AI as editor and thought-partner, especially late in the process, but cautions that early outlines can foreclose original thinking. He then invites teachers to think the unthinkable about reading and writing as primary input and output, and recommends small cohorts running structured experiments because school-level AI committees have stalled.
points: Teachers need evidence-based rationales for unassisted writing rather than bans, and Potkalitsky proposes knowledge-constitution as the most persuasive and immediate one.
His informal classroom experiment found that students allowed to research online generated little original evidence, while the unassisted class produced items missing from the research list.
He sees LLMs as most useful at the start and end of the writing process, but warns that early AI-generated outlines can close down students’ own thinking.
He urges educators to think the unthinkable about reading and writing as primary input and output, while still doubting school can do without them.
Because school AI committees fizzled after the early fall, he recommends small departmental cohorts testing hypotheses with real research questions.
quotes: Today's students need more than just prescriptions or prohibitions of specific AI practices. They require thoughtful, persuasive, and evidence-based rationales. These rationales should guide both classroom interactions and daily engagements with Gen AI.
Notably, both schools of thought as first-wave reactive responses to the widespread accessibility of Gen AI under-theorize both rationales and practices.

Each time a student sets aside Gen AI, particularly during the early stages of the writing process, and draws on their first-order and second-order memory in order to synthesize new ideas in the form of written expression, they are involved in the work of knowledge-constitution, which plays a central part in the development of critical thinking, meta-cognition, ethical evaluation, organizational awareness, and relational analysis.

In the second case, students initially struggled to get going, but then created a list of evidence that included 3 items that did not appear on the research list. The tenor of the lesson was completely different as students work more creatively and collaboratively toward shared solutions.

When a student asks a LLM to generate an outline on a particular topic, that projection can serve either to open up new fields of discourse or close them down depending upon a student’s past experiences and skills and competencies, the teacher’s framing of these utilizations, and the technology’s structural properties.

In the face of these institutional barriers and tensions points, I advise teachers to work collaboratively in small cohorts to test out different hypotheses about the value, impact, and efficacy of AI-responsive classroom strategies and approaches.
